name: Gustave Caillebotte
teaser: The Impressionist who financed the movement and painted it better than most — his rain-soaked Paris streets, floor scrapers, and the plunging balconies of Haussmann's Paris are masterpieces of modern life. He also collected his friends' paintings and gave them to the state.

exploreAction.targetName: Paris Street; Rainy Day (Art Institute of Chicago) — the couple
exploreAction.instruction: A rainy boulevard under a grey sky: umbrellas, cobblestones glistening, and a couple in the foreground walking toward you. Look at the perspective — the street converges exactly, the figures are cropped like a photograph. Caillebotte was the Impressionist with a ruler.

name: Armand Guillaumin
teaser: The rugged Impressionist of hills and quarries — a postal clerk who painted on weekends until he won the lottery and painted full-time. His landscapes of the Creuse valley and his boldly colored rocks made him a bridge to the Fauves.

exploreAction.targetName: The Creuse valley landscapes or Sunset at Ivry
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the color: Guillaumin painted rock faces in violet, orange, and green that the Impressionists' palette barely allowed. His friend Cézanne envied his energy. He won the lottery at 49 and painted mountains for the next 35 years — the happiest ending in art history.

name: Frédéric Bazille
teaser: The generous young painter who shared his studio and his money with Monet, Renoir, and Sisley — and died in the Franco-Prussian War at 28, before his promise was kept. His Family Reunion and Studio in the Rue de la Condamine are quiet masterpieces.

exploreAction.targetName: The Studio in the Rue de la Condamine (Musée d'Orsay) — the friends
exploreAction.instruction: A Paris studio with the artist at his easel and his friends — including Monet, Manet, and Renoir — chatting by the window. Look at the light, the space, the ambition. Bazille painted the Impressionists before they were famous; he was their first patron and their first loss.

name: Eva Gonzalès
teaser: The only formal student of Édouard Manet — a gifted painter of women, fans, and boudoirs who died in childbirth at 34. Her portraits and domestic scenes are sharp, elegant, and quietly modernist, caught between Manet's influence and her own voice.

exploreAction.targetName: A Box at the Theatre or the White Nightgown portraits
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how Gonzalès handles white: a woman in a lace nightgown, a fan, a morning light — paint that is both soft and precise. She exhibited with the Impressionists and held her own against her famous teacher. A career cut short, a voice half-heard.

name: Marie Bracquemond
teaser: The least-known of the 'three great ladies of Impressionism' — a painter of gardens, picnics, and terraces whose luminous work her husband, the etcher Félix Bracquemond, tried to suppress. She stopped painting at 60, exhausted by the fight.

exploreAction.targetName: On the Terrace at Sèvres or Under the Lamp
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the light on the terrace: a woman reads in a garden that glows green and gold. Bracquemond studied with Ingres, discovered Impressionism through Monet, and made it her own — bright, warm, and full of air. Then read about her husband; the silence is part of the story.

name: Henri-Edmond Cross
teaser: The Neo-Impressionist who took pointillism to the south of France and loosened it into ribbons of color — his luminous landscapes of Saint-Tropez beaches and pine groves inspired Matisse and the Fauves. His name was a joke he kept (his real name was Delacroix).

exploreAction.targetName: The Golden Isles or the Saint-Clair landscapes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the dabs: not the tight dots of Seurat, but long, relaxed strokes of color that shimmer like stained glass. Cross painted the Mediterranean as a dream of warmth — pink sand, blue sea, green pines. Matisse called his work 'a revelation.'

name: Maximilien Luce
teaser: The anarchist Neo-Impressionist who painted factories, strikes, and Paris in dots — his industrial landscapes of the working Seine are pointillism with a political heart. He was jailed in 1894 for his anarchist friends; he painted jail from inside.

exploreAction.targetName: The Factory at Charleroi or the strikes paintings
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how Luce turns an ironworks into a symphony of dots — smoke, flame, and workers all vibrating with color. He believed beauty belonged to working people. His chimneys are as heroic as any cathedral, and his crowds are full of individuals.

name: Paul Signac
teaser: The Neo-Impressionist who painted the sea in dots and sailed through the ports of France in his yacht — his harbors, bridges, and Mediterranean skies are pointillism at its most joyful. He wrote the movement's manifesto and financed its painters.

exploreAction.targetName: The Port of Saint-Tropez or the Venice series
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the color logic: Signac placed complementary colors side by side so they mix in your eye — red dots next to green, blue next to orange. His Venice is a mosaic of light on water. He was rich, generous, and relentlessly happy — the anti-starving-artist.

name: Théo van Rysselberghe
teaser: The Belgian Neo-Impressionist who painted the elegant Mediterranean — his portraits, beaches, and the famous Reading by the Sea are pointillism refined into luxury. He brought Seurat's dots to the high society of Brussels and the Côte d'Azur.

exploreAction.targetName: Reading by the Sea (1903) — the couple
exploreAction.instruction: A woman reads on a rock while a man watches the sea — painted in thousands of dots that blend into a warm, sun-drenched moment. Look at the rhythm of the dots on the water: they ripple like real waves. Van Rysselberghe made technique disappear into atmosphere.

name: Ivan Generalić
teaser: The Croatian naif painter of Hlebine who painted village winters, floods, and fairytale landscapes in flat, folkloric color — he is the founder of the famous Croatian naive art school, discovered by a painter who saw his drawings through a fence.

exploreAction.targetName: The Deer Wedding or the winter village scenes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the snow: Generalić painted Croatian winters as white kingdoms full of detail — horses, sleds, smoke, and tiny human dramas. His Deer Wedding turns a hunt into a fairytale procession. He painted on glass and with enamel, and his world is a folk tale told in paint.

name: Franjo Mraz
teaser: A founder of the Hlebine naive school — a Croatian farmer-painter whose scenes of threshing, weddings, and fairs are painted with the directness of folk art and the joy of a man who painted because he loved it.

exploreAction.targetName: The Wedding or the harvest scenes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the flat perspective and the honest details: a village wedding with musicians, a harvest with sweating backs. Mraz never went to art school; he painted his life and his neighbors' lives in bright, confident color. The folk tradition, alive in oil.

name: Niko Pirosmani
teaser: The Georgian naif who painted animals, feasts, and moons on black oilcloth — a self-taught wanderer who traded paintings for food and died in poverty. His black backgrounds and tender animals made him a cult figure of the avant-garde; the dadaists and futurists adored him.

exploreAction.targetName: The Giraffe or the Feast scenes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at The Giraffe: a solitary giraffe stands on a black field, its spots painted with flat precision — no one knows why he painted it, and it's one of the most beloved images in Georgian art. Pirosmani painted his signs, his feasts, and his animals on whatever he had.

name: Grandma Moses
teaser: The American folk painter who started at 76 — Anna Mary Robertson Moses painted her childhood farms, sugaring seasons, and village squares in flat, bright memory-color. She became the most famous American painter of the 1950s, beloved by presidents and children alike.

exploreAction.targetName: The Old Checkered House or Sugaring Off — the seasons
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the flat, cheerful scenes: horses, sleighs, maple sugaring, a harvest — all remembered from her own 19th-century childhood. Moses painted from memory, never from life, and her memory was warm. She lived to 101 and painted for 25 years.

name: Morris Hirshfield
teaser: The Polish-American slipper manufacturer who took up painting at 66 after illness — his flat, patterned tigers, nudes, and landscapes are among the strangest and most treasured works of outsider art. MoMA exhibited him; critics argued about him for decades.

exploreAction.targetName: Tiger or the Angora Cat paintings
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the pattern: Hirshfield painted a tiger with stripes that ripple like fabric — he had spent his life in the garment trade, and it shows. His figures are flat, frontal, and mesmerizing. The Surrealists called him one of their own; he called himself a businessman who painted.

name: Bill Traylor
teaser: The Alabama artist who began drawing at 85 — a former enslaved man who sat on a Montgomery sidewalk and drew the city and his memories in pencil and paint on cardboard. His flat, powerful figures of men, animals, and events are now a cornerstone of American art.

exploreAction.targetName: The figures and animals on cardboard — the energy
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the simplification: a man with a bottle, a dog, a snake — drawn with a few bold shapes and a lifetime of observation. Traylor drew what he saw from the street and what he remembered from the plantation. He died in 1949, unknown; his work now hangs in the Met.

name: Clementine Hunter
teaser: The Louisiana plantation worker who painted her life on whatever she could find — window shades, bottles, jugs — and became the first African American artist to have a solo exhibition at a Louisiana museum. Her cotton fields, baptisms, and zinnias are full of life.

exploreAction.targetName: The cotton-picking scenes or the zinnia still lifes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the flat, joyful figures: women in bright dresses, baptisms in the river, harvests in the fields. Hunter painted what she lived for 100 years. She said she 'just painted,' and her 'just' contains everything: memory, celebration, and a world made bright by hand.

name: Joseph Yoakum
teaser: The self-taught American who drew landscapes of places he claimed to have seen — his curling, contour-lined mountains, forests, and oceans flow like topographic maps of the imagination. He said he traveled the world in circuses and trains; art critics say it doesn't matter.

exploreAction.targetName: The mountain and landscape drawings — the lines
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the flowing contour lines: Yoakum drew landforms as continuous spirals and waves, every inch of the paper worked. His colors are gentle, his places impossible. The Museum of Modern Art collected him; his landscapes look like somewhere you've dreamed.

name: Minnie Evans
teaser: The North Carolina gatekeeper-turned-visionary who painted gardens of paradise in ink and wax crayon — her symmetrical, jewel-toned faces and flowers, inspired by dreams and visions, made her a star of outsider art. She said God told her to draw.

exploreAction.targetName: The visionary faces and garden drawings — the symmetry
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the mirror symmetry: faces within faces, flowers within flowers, eyes everywhere. Evans worked as a gatekeeper at Airlie Gardens and said the visions began in her 40s. Her drawings are like windows into a paradise she was instructed to paint.

name: James Hampton
teaser: The janitor who built a throne for God — a Washington, D.C. custodian who spent 14 years constructing The Throne of the Third Heaven from tin foil, cardboard, and light bulbs, a glittering altar 180 pieces strong, now a national treasure at the Smithsonian.

exploreAction.targetName: The Throne of the Third Heaven (Smithsonian American Art Museum) — the foil
exploreAction.instruction: Walk around the glittering structure: throne, altar, crowns, and banners all wrapped in foil and inscribed with Hampton's private scripture. He worked at night in a rented garage and left a note: 'This is the True and Living God.' Found after his death, it's one of the great works of American vision.

name: Simon Rodia
teaser: The Italian immigrant who spent 33 years building the Watts Towers — a cluster of spires, ships, and arches made of steel, wire, and mortar, decorated with broken bottles, seashells, and tiles. He built it alone, by hand, with no plans, and left when it was done.

exploreAction.targetName: The Watts Towers (Los Angeles) — walk inside
exploreAction.instruction: Walk under the spires and look at the details embedded in the mortar: bottle bottoms glowing green, seashell spirals, bits of mirror. Rodia built it without scaffolding, without drawings, working from the ground up with a window-washer's belt. He called it 'just something I had to do.'
